questions.q: What is the real first diagnostic move once the CI log reports the unique test failure?
options: Re-reading customers.sql from scratch with no other information
Querying the specific duplicated customer_id rows directly, using the failing test's own output as the starting point
Immediately reverting the entire pull request without investigating
Rebuilding the whole Snowflake warehouse from scratch
questions.explain: The failing test already names the problem (duplicate customer_id rows); querying those specific rows is the concrete, evidence-based starting point.

questions.q: How does the lineage graph help confirm the diagnosis in this lesson?
options: It shows exactly how much the Snowflake bill increased
It shows customers now has a new, direct edge to stg_jaffle_shop__payments that bypasses int_orders__payment_summary — visible proof of what changed
It automatically fixes the broken SQL
It has no role in diagnosing this specific incident
questions.explain: A new edge appearing in the generated lineage graph is visual confirmation matching what the failing test already pointed to.

questions.q: What is the actual fix applied to customers.sql?
options: Adding a DISTINCT keyword to the broken join to remove duplicate rows
Reverting to Lesson 9's original design: routing back through orders (which already resolved payments via int_orders__payment_summary) instead of joining payments a second time
Deleting the customer_id column entirely from the model
Changing the unique test's severity to warn so it stops blocking the build
questions.explain: The real fix recognizes the original architecture already computed lifetime_value correctly — the fanout came from an unnecessary second join at the wrong grain.

questions.q: Why does this lesson distinguish a "correct fix" from a "passing fix"?
options: They are the same thing with no meaningful difference
A passing fix might just satisfy the test; a correct fix addresses the real design problem — this fix restores the architecture that was already accurate
A passing fix is always faster to write than a correct fix
Only a correct fix is allowed to be committed to git
questions.explain: The lesson deliberately highlights that lowering the test's severity or suppressing it would merely pass CI without fixing the underlying inflated numbers.

questions.q: What happens after the fix is pushed as a new commit to the same pull request?
options: Nothing automatic happens; CI must be manually re-triggered by an administrator
ci.yml re-triggers automatically, dbt build runs again, the unique test passes with zero results, and the required status check clears, re-enabling the merge button
A brand new pull request must be opened to re-test the fix
The fix is deployed directly to PROD without going through CI again
questions.explain: Pushing a new commit automatically re-runs the required workflow, and a passing result clears the gate from Lesson 21.
